passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of three novel attentional training protocols on reaction time in a laboratory setting. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no training, and three treatment groups (A, B, and C) that each received a different training protocol. After a 4‑week intervention period, participants completed a computerized visual‑search task while their reaction times were recorded. The mean reaction times (in milliseconds) and standard deviations for each group are presented in Table 1. The data suggest that all training protocols reduced reaction time relative to the control, with Treatment B yielding the greatest improvement. The researchers plan to analyze whether the differences among treatments are statistically significant and to explore the underlying neural mechanisms. This study exemplifies how controlled experimental designs can isolate the effects of specific interventions on cognitive performance.
stem: Which group had the fastest average reaction time?
explanation: The mean reaction time for Treatment B is 1050 ms, which is lower (i.e., faster) than the other groups (Control 1200 ms, Treatment A 1100 ms, Treatment C 1150 ms). Lower reaction time indicates faster performance.
trap: Choosing the Control or Treatment C by reading larger numbers as faster; a lower mean reaction time in ms means faster performance.

stem: Which experimental design best tests the effect of the treatments on reaction time?
explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) randomly assigns participants to treatment or control groups, controlling for confounding variables and allowing causal inference about the effect of the treatments on reaction time.
trap: Assuming that a cross‑sectional survey can determine causality.

stem: Calculate the percent reduction in mean reaction time from Control to Treatment B.
explanation: Percent reduction = (1200 – 1050) / 1200 × 100 = 150 / 1200 × 100 = 12.5%. Thus option B is correct.
trap: Using Treatment A's 100 ms drop (8.3%) or dividing by the treatment mean instead of the control mean of 1200 ms; the denominator is the control.

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by Table 1 and the passage?

options.A: Treatment B had the lowest mean reaction time of the four groups.
options.B: Every treatment group had a lower mean reaction time than the control group.
options.C: The mean reaction time of Treatment C was 50 ms lower than that of the control group.
options.D: The differences among the group means were shown to be statistically significant.

explanation: Correct: The table reports only means and SDs, and the passage says the researchers plan to test significance, so significance has not been shown. Why the others are wrong: A) 1050 ms is the lowest mean. B) 1100, 1050 and 1150 ms are all below 1200 ms. C) 1200 − 1150 = 50 ms.
trap: Treating a visible difference in means as proof of statistical significance.

stem: Which statement about variability is supported by Table 1?

options.A: The control group had the largest SD.
options.B: Treatment B had the smallest SD.
options.C: All four groups had identical SDs.
options.D: Treatment A had the largest SD.

explanation: Correct: Treatment B's SD of 130 ms is the smallest of the four (150, 140, 130, 160). Why the others are wrong: A) Treatment C (160 ms) had a larger SD than control (150 ms). C) the SDs are 150, 140, 130 and 160 ms. D) Treatment A's 140 ms is not the largest.
trap: Picking the control group as most variable because it had the slowest mean, overlooking that Treatment C's SD (160 ms) exceeds the control's (150 ms).
